messages.body_plain:
Hi Zhong-wen,

Good question. First, re the conversion, just to be clear, that paper I sent said about 3.4 cal / mg. There are about 1.43 mg / l O2 so the conversion from ml O2 / h to J / h is  3.4 * 1.4 * 4.186, i.e. about 20. To convert to watts (J/s) you then divide by 3600 to get 0.0056.

Re the differences you saw between Qmet and the outputted O2, that is because there are some caps on the allowable metabolic rate in the heat budget calculation - see code below. So the metabolic rate is not allowed to go to zero, but capped at 0.01 W, and when the animal is getting too hot it's capped at what it would be at 0.5 deg C above the VTmax.

When you put rain-limited activity on, it wasn't getting as hot. Hope that clears things up.

All the best,
Mike

       IF(TC .GT. 50)THEN
C       CAP METABOLIC RATE EQUATION WITH MAX OF TC = 50
        QMETAB = 0.0056*10.**(MR_3*50)*MR_1*GMASS**MR_2
        GOTO 101
       ENDIF
       IF(TC.LE.TPREF)THEN
        IF(TC.GE.1.0)THEN
C        ACCEPTABLE TEMPERATURE RANGE
         QMETAB=0.0056*10.**(MR_3*TC)*MR_1*GMASS**MR_2
        ELSE
         QMETAB = 0.01
        ENDIF
       ELSE
C       TOO HOT
C       ALLOWING TCORE TO BE A LITTLE HIGHER THAN TMAX PREFERRED SO THAT THERMOREGULATION
C       BEHAVIORS WILL BE INVOKED TO SELECT MORE MODERATE MICROCLIMATE CONDITIONS
        QMETAB = 0.0056*10.**(MR_3*(TMAXPR+0.5))*MR_1*GMASS**MR_2
       ENDIF

I didn't totally follow your question. But, yes, I put it there so that you could simulate e.g. a frog that only comes out after rain. Turning it on may lead to higher body temperatures because it might be warmer in the retreat (underground) than out in the open. The rainact argument just adds an extra condition to activity, i.e. it has to be raining above the threshold amount on that day, the threshold being rainfall in mm. But, I also had code in the evaporation subroutine, SEVAP, to make humidity 99% when rainact was on and it was raining. I've just removed that code because it may not be a good assumption for some cases. It is better that you modify the metout/shadmet matrices manually to change humidity during rain events before passing them to the ectotherm model. That will also modify the body temperatures you get, because without the assumption of 99% RH, they may end up with lower body temperatures due to evaporative cooling.

All the best,
Mike

Hi Adam,
The horizon angles can be calculated from a DEM and passed to the microclimate model (argument 'hori') and this will capture effects of nearby mountains on direct beam solar (or you could use it to simulate the effects e.g. of a wall).
e.g.
      elev <- raster::extract(dem, c(lon, lat))[1]
      xy <- data.frame(x = lon, y = lat)
      sp::coordinates(xy) = ~x + y
      sp::proj4string(xy) = "+init=epsg:4326"
      xy <- as.data.frame(sp::spTransform(xy, raster::crs(dem)))
      ha36 <- 0
      for (i in 0:35) {
        har <- horizonangle(dem, i * 10, raster::res(dem)[1])
        ha36[i + 1] <- atan(raster::extract(har, xy)) * (180/pi)
      }
      hori <- spline(x = ha36, n = 24, method =  'periodic')$y
      hori[hori < 0] <- 0
      hori[hori > 90] <- 90

messages.subject: Re: Issue with micro_era5 in a loop: "Error in R_nc4_open: Too many open files"
messages.subject_clean: Issue with micro_era5 in a loop: "Error in R_nc4_open: Too many open files"
messages.body_plain:
I know this was a while ago, but I've come up with a decent solution for this problem without needing to use a for loop. Restarting the R session allows R to clear all of the open connections to the nc files, so we need a way to allow R to restart the session while keeping the loop going. The package rstudioapi has the function restartSession(), and inside the restartSession function you can tell it to call to your current script and run it again after restarting. If you save the iteration number that you are currently on plus one (so if you're on iteration 1, you save a 2) to another directory before you restart the session, R will check on that number after restarting and keep going right where it left off (as long as you use the variable you saved it as in place of the looping variable).

See example code here, which I took from this link (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48305203/restart-r-session-without-interrupting-the-for-loop):

#Save an the iteration as a separate .RData file in the working directory.
 iter <- 1 save(iter, file="iter.RData")

Create a script which calls itself for a certain number of iterations. Save the following script as "test_script.R"
###load iteration
library(rstudioapi)
load("iter.RData")
###insert function here.
time_now <- Sys.time()
###save output of function to a file.
save(time_now, file=paste0("time_", iter, ".Rdata"))
###update iteration
iter <- iter+1
save(iter, file="iter.RData")
###restart session calling the script again
if(iter < 5){
restartSession(command='source("test_script.R")') }

messages.subject: Issue with panting costs in endotherm model
messages.subject_clean: Issue with panting costs in endotherm model
messages.body_plain:
Dear endotherm model users,
Liang Ma just alerted me to an error (thanks!) in the coding of the panting costs in endoR_devel and in the associated endoR functions, which actually resulted in them being subtracted rather than added (blush). It is fixed now and pushed to github. This issue would mean that if you were simulating panting and had left the PANT_MULT at its default value, you would have underestimated the actual heat load a little bit (by 5%) and hence underestimated the water costs of this.
My apologies for any problems this has caused.
All the best,
Mike
